proposed_features.description: The overall size of the bird's body, from head to tail, relative to the frame and background elements, which helps distinguish larger corvids from smaller birds.
The dominant color of the feathers, which varies from dark gray to black, and can include iridescence or dullness, aiding in differentiation between species.
The shape of the beak, including its curvature, thickness, and tip, which varies from stout and hooked to slender and pointed, indicating different feeding adaptations.
The color of the beak, which can range from black to pale or yellowish, providing a visual cue for species identification.
The relative length of the tail compared to the body, which can be short, medium, or long, and helps distinguish between species with different flight and perching behaviors.
The shape of the tail when viewed from the side or back, such as rounded, forked, or squared, which is a key morphological trait.
The position of the wings relative to the body, whether folded tightly against the body or slightly raised, indicating posture and potential for flight.
The shape of the head, including the prominence of the crown, forehead, and nape, which can be rounded, angular, or crested, aiding in species distinction.
The color of the eye, which can vary from dark to lighter shades, and may be visible in some images, providing a subtle but useful discriminative feature.
The relative length of the legs compared to the body, which can be short, medium, or long, influencing the bird's stance and habitat preference.
The visual texture of the feathers, ranging from smooth and glossy to rough and matte, which can indicate health, species, or environmental conditions.
The type of surface the bird is perched on, such as a branch, rock, post, or ground, which can correlate with habitat and behavior.
